transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-24 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Emma Carter (Redwood AE), Liam Nguyen (Redwood SE), Saira Hussain (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (CTO, Vertex), Maya Lopez (ML Eng), Oliver Chen (SRE), Tanya Rivera (PM)

Summary: short workshop to lock down POC acceptance gates and how we fold Vertex's scripts into the Redwood harness. Lots of focus on streaming vs non-streaming, KV cache warmup and what counts as a pass for them.

[00:00] Emma: alright everyone thanks for joining, uh quick roll call and then we'll jump in. we have a pretty packed agenda, facing the harness integration and success criteria.
[00:12] Raj: yep thanks emma, tat's raj here. excited to see what 'redwood' can do, we got a tight timeline, october launch window if possible.
[00:20] Maya: hey team, maya here. i'll be driving the scripts and a lot of the model comparison pieces.
[00:27] Oliver: ollie here, i'll be doing infra and the runbook with you all. a couple network Qs up front.
[00:35] Emma: great, so high level goal — two week pilot to validate throughput and tail latency for our production traffic slices. we recommend breaking tests into ramp / sustained / spike phases. does that map to vertex's acceptance gates?
[00:50] Raj: yes, our product team cares about p95 and p99 on UIs, the PM also cares about consistent tail under heavy load. threshold numbers: ideally p95 < 250ms, p99 < 600ms for typical prompts, error rate below 0.5%.
[01:12] Liam: ok noted. quick clar — are those numbers for streaming responses (server-sent events) or non-streaming full-output generation? sometimes that changes metrics.
[01:22] Tanya: primarily UI uses streaming for progressive render, but we have batch jobs that will do non-streaming for long-form generation. so we need both.
[01:31] Saira: perfect, so we'll treat streaming as the primary latency path and non-streaming as throughput-heavy. couple of things to call out: streaming reduces perceived latency but increases concurrency because of open connections.
[01:50] Maya: and we have stateful sessions, so KV cache behavior is important. we want to see warmup behavior — how many initial requests until K V cache is effectively hot?
[02:03] Liam: yep, KV cache warmup is one of the main acceptance gates. we'll propose a warm-up plan: pre-populate common prefixes with synthetic replay, then run a warmed sustained run for 2 hours to validate steady-state metrics.
[02:20] Oliver: when you say pre-populate, is that a manual replay or can the harness do that? our concern is realistic token distributions.
[02:28] Emma: the harness supports both; we can replay customer's scripts verbatim to approximate production and the adapter can optionally pre-warm K V cache with a headless warmup mode. we'll share the adapter template.
[02:43] Raj: sounds good. also curious about batching — we get higher throughput with batching but higher latency per token. what's the tradeoff here?
[02:52] Liam: right — we usually recommend dynamic batching with a cap. for interactive UIs keep batch size small e.g., 4 or 8, for non-streaming batch jobs go up to maybe 32 depending on model. profiling will tell us exact sweet spot.
[03:08] Maya: our token distribution: median 120 tokens, 90th 420 tokens, long tail 1-2k. we can share histogram.
[03:18] Emma: please do. that will drive kernel selection / quantization suggestions.
[03:24] [crosstalk] Tanya: question about model variants — we have a 'large' and 'medium' in prod, and we may experiment with quantized variants for cost.
[03:34] Saira: we will include quantized model runs; Redwood has model profiles for 8-bit and 4-bit. note: 4-bit sometimes increases latency for short sequences due to less optimized kernels, we should check.
[03:50] Raj: network and security — SOC2 and KMS are mandatory. can we get audit logs for every inference call?
[03:58] Emma: yes we can stream audit logs to your SIEM, and KMS integration is available for private deployment. log retention policies we can configure; we'll include SOC2 attestation docs in the followup.
[04:15] Oliver: about network — we'll be using a V-P-C peered setup for the pilot, need to confirm egress and inbound ports. can you share the port list?
[04:25] Liam: yes, we'll send a minimal list; typically TLS 443 outbound for hosted but for private deployment there are internal ports for health checks, gRPC, and the agent.
[04:39] Emma: moving onto instrumentation: what telemetry do you need? token-level latencies, model variant breakdown, batch sizes, error counts?
[04:48] Maya: all of that, plus memory and GPU utilization per node. we want to understand cost vs latency curves.
[04:57] Liam: we'll enable per-token tracing and aggregate to p50/p95/p99. note recordings will be sampled to control storage.
[05:06] Raj: for acceptance, besides p95/p99 and error rates we also want throughput guarantees: sustained 400 qps with occasional spikes to 1200 qps for 2 minutes without error rate > 1.5%.
[05:20] Saira: okay we'll define the ramp: 0 -> 400 in 10 minutes, hold 60 minutes, 3x spike test to 1200 for 2 minutes, then back down. we'll capture cold-start metrics when we scale from zero as well.
[05:33] Oliver: cold starts are big for us — how does redwood handle instance spin-up and state reuse? does it keep standby pools?
[05:42] Emma: Dedicated mode has warm pools and pre-warming options; hosted mode uses fast scaling with some cold start variance. for this pilot we can reserve a small warm pool to minimize cold starts.
[05:55] Maya: timeline question — we want results and a go/no-go within two weeks. is that feasible?
[06:01] Liam: yes, two week pilot is typical: week 1 onboarding + warm-up and preliminary runs; week 2 sustained runs, optimizations and final acceptance.
[06:10] Raj: what about cost visibility — we need cost per 1M tokens estimate and the ability to cap spend.
[06:18] Emma: we'll provide an estimated unit cost split by model variant and streaming vs non-streaming. we also support quotas and alerts to cap spend.
[06:27] Tanya: about harness integration — how invasive is the adapter? we want minimal changes to our scripts and auth flow.
[06:33] Liam: adapter pattern is thin: a small shim (python/Node) that translates your script format into the harness API. authentication can be SSO or API key; for private deployment we can use mutual TLS.
[06:46] Maya: any gotchas for streaming? we use SSE in the front end and we need chunked progressive tokens.
[06:52] Saira: streaming is supported via SSE / websockets. the main operational overhead is keeping connections open and handling partial failures; harness will retry idempotent streams with backoff, but for stateful sessions you need deterministic fallthrough policies.
[07:10] Raj: what's a realistic pass/fail checklist?
[07:14] Emma: draft checklist: p95 < 250ms (streaming), p99 < 600ms, error rate < 0.5%, sustained throughput 400 qps, spike behavior tolerable up to 1200 qps with graceful degradation, KV cache warm within first N calls (we'll quantify), and telemetry + logs available to your SRE.
[07:30] Oliver: we also want a memory/GPU utilization baseline — e.g. GPU mem < 90% during sustained runs to avoid OOM.
[07:37] Liam: noted. we'll include GPU OOM and OOM-kill thresholds in the runbook.
[07:43] Maya: on scripts — i'll send 10 canonical prompts and some long-form templates. also include expected label/answer so we can measure quality regressions during quantized runs.
[07:56] Emma: perfect — that will also let us add accuracy/quality as a soft gate.
[08:01] [long pause — file transfer noise in call]
[08:05] Tanya: question on rollout — after pilot, we may want dedicated capacity for predictable latency, what are the contract lengths and burst options?
[08:14] Emma: Dedicated is monthly/annual reserved capacity with burst options; we'll include a pricing sketch. for immediate pilot we'll use reserved ephemeral capacity for solidarity.
[08:26] Raj: any competitor concerns? our infra team looked at Anthropic and openai — main differences were price and control. we've already tried an in-house GPU pool but maintaining it was costly.
[08:40] Emma: understandable. that's why we push observability and cost tooling — so you can see tradeoffs in the runbook.
[08:48] Oliver: network question follow-up — do you need inbound IP allowlist?
[08:52] Liam: yes we'll provide CIDR ranges and can support fixed egress IPs for hosted endpoints or direct peering for private.
[09:00] Maya: ok last bit on evaluation rubric — can we add quality checks? like sample-based exact-match and embed-similarity for a small eval set.
[09:09] Saira: yes we recommend a small eval harness that runs at each benchmark stage to ensure quantized runs don't regress. we'll include that in the runbook.
[09:20] Emma: wrap up — recap of action items and next steps, agreed to schedule the SRE benchmark on oct 5th and for vertex to send scripts by sept 29th.
[09:32] Raj: thanks everyone, we'll follow up internally and get you the assets.
[09:36] Tanya: thanks, bye.

End of transcript.
